subproblem.title: Differentiation of the radial cutoff mass under the integral sign (step 5)
subproblem.statement: Let N ∈ ℕ, let μ be a measure on ℝ^N = Euclidean N (Borel σ-algebra) and y ∈ ℝ^N. Let h : ℝ^N → ℝ be continuous, and let φ : ℝ → ℝ be of class C¹ with φ(s) = 0 for every s ≥ A², where A > 0. Let R ∈ ℝ with μ(B_R(y)) < ∞, where B_R(y) = closedBall y R. Then for every t₀ > 0 with t₀·A < R, the function t ↦ ∫ φ(|z − y|²/t²)·h(z) dμ(z) (Bochner integral) has derivative ∫ φ'(|z − y|²/t₀²)·(−2|z − y|²/t₀³)·h(z) dμ(z) at t₀, where φ' := deriv φ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Euclidean N)) (y : Euclidean N) (h : Euclidean N → ℝ) (φ : ℝ → ℝ) (A R t₀ : ℝ), Continuous h → ContDiff ℝ 1 φ → 0 < A → (∀ s, A ^ 2 ≤ s → φ s = 0) → μ (closedBall y R) ≠ ∞ → 0 < t₀ → t₀ * A < R → HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ ↦ ∫ z, φ (‖z - y‖ ^ 2 / t ^ 2) * h z ∂μ) (∫ z, deriv φ (‖z - y‖ ^ 2 / t₀ ^ 2) * (-2 * ‖z - y‖ ^ 2 / t₀ ^ 3) * h z ∂μ) t₀
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: step 5 of the parent proof (differentiation under the integral sign in Simon 8.3.5), for an arbitrary measure μ that is finite on B_R(y) and an arbitrary continuous weight h.
Notation. B_r(y) := closedBall y r. For z ∈ ℝ^N put w := z − y and φ' := deriv φ. For t ∈ ℝ and z ∈ ℝ^N:
  F(t,z) := φ(‖w‖²/t²)·h(z),  F'(t,z) := φ'(‖w‖²/t²)·(−2‖w‖²/t³)·h(z).
K := B_R(y).

1. Constants. Since t₀ > 0 and A > 0, R > t₀A > 0, so t₀ < R/A. Put a := t₀/2 and b := (t₀ + R/A)/2. Then 0 < a < t₀ < b and bA < R. K is compact (a closed ball in ℝ^N) and measurable, and μ(K) < ∞ by hypothesis.

2. Cut-off facts.
 (i) If s > A², then φ vanishes on the open neighbourhood (A², ∞) of s, so φ'(s) = 0 (Filter.EventuallyEq.deriv_eq).
 (ii) If t ∈ [a, b] and z ∉ K, then ‖w‖ > R > bA ≥ tA > 0. Hence ‖w‖² > (tA)², i.e. ‖w‖²/t² > A². So φ(‖w‖²/t²) = 0 and, by (i), φ'(‖w‖²/t²) = 0. Thus F(t,z) = F'(t,z) = 0.

3. Continuity. φ and φ' are continuous (φ is C¹), and h is continuous. So for every t > 0 (in particular every t ∈ [a, b]) the maps z ↦ F(t,z) and z ↦ F'(t,z) are continuous, hence strongly measurable. Moreover (t,z) ↦ F'(t,z) is continuous on [a, b] × K, because t ≥ a > 0 there, so no division by zero occurs.

4. Domination. [a, b] × K is compact, so there is C ≥ 0 with |F'(t,z)| ≤ C for all (t,z) ∈ [a, b] × K. Explicitly one may take C := L·(2R²/a³)·H, where L bounds |φ'| on [0, R²/a²] and H bounds |h| on K: for (t,z) ∈ [a,b] × K, ‖w‖ ≤ R and t ≥ a, so ‖w‖²/t² ∈ [0, R²/a²] and 2‖w‖²/t³ ≤ 2R²/a³. Put bound(z) := C·1_K(z). By 2(ii), |F'(t,z)| ≤ bound(z) for all z and all t ∈ (a, b). bound is μ-integrable, since ∫ bound dμ = C·μ(K) < ∞.

5. Integrability of F(t₀,·). F(t₀,·) is continuous, hence bounded on the compact set K by some C₀. Since μ(K) < ∞, it is integrable on K (Measure.integrableOn_of_bounded). By 2(ii), with t₀ ∈ [a, b], it vanishes outside K. Hence it is μ-integrable (IntegrableOn.integrable_of_forall_notMem_eq_zero).

6. Pointwise derivative. Fix z and let t ≠ 0. By the quotient rule, s(t) := ‖w‖²/t² has derivative −2‖w‖²/t³ at t. φ is differentiable, so by the chain rule t ↦ φ(s(t)) has derivative φ'(s(t))·(−2‖w‖²/t³). Multiplying by the constant h(z), t ↦ F(t,z) has derivative F'(t,z) at every t ∈ (a, b).

7. Conclusion. (a, b) is a neighbourhood of t₀. Apply differentiation under the integral sign (Mathlib hasDerivAt_integral_of_dominated_loc_of_deriv_le with s := (a, b)). Its hypotheses hold:
 - F(t,·) is a.e.-strongly measurable for every t in the neighbourhood (a, b) of t₀ (step 3);
 - F(t₀,·) is integrable (step 5);
 - F'(t₀,·) is a.e.-strongly measurable (step 3);
 - ‖F'(t,z)‖ ≤ bound(z) for all z and t ∈ (a, b), and bound is integrable (step 4);
 - t ↦ F(t,z) has derivative F'(t,z) for all z and t ∈ (a, b) (step 6).
 So t ↦ ∫ F(t,z) dμ(z) has derivative ∫ F'(t₀,z) dμ(z) at t₀. That is the claim. ∎
proof_key_steps: a := t₀/2 and b := (t₀ + R/A)/2 give 0 < a < t₀ < b and bA < R; K := B_R(y) is compact with μ(K) < ∞
φ' = 0 on (A², ∞); for t ∈ [a,b] and z ∉ K, ‖z−y‖²/t² > A², so F(t,z) = F'(t,z) = 0
F' is continuous on [a,b] × K, hence bounded by some C; bound := C·1_K is μ-integrable
F(t₀,·) is continuous, bounded on K and zero off K, hence integrable
∂_t F(t,z) = φ'(‖z−y‖²/t²)(−2‖z−y‖²/t³)h(z) by the quotient and chain rules
